### c1-1M-NaClO4-EC-PC
评估建议：The candidate matches the literature electrolyte that establishes the ~250 mAh/g no-plating HC limit at -20 C, so it is a valid starting point, but the same source reports fast full-cell capacity fading at -20 C with this electrolyte and explicitly calls for electrolyte optimization; therefore it is not yet demonstrated as an appropriate low-temperature full-cell electrolyte and no recommendation is made.
任务要求与已有依据（模型语义判断，程序核验出处）：
- Electrolyte salt is NaClO4 at 1.0 mol/L：The paper states '1M NaClO4 solution' was applied as electrolyte for the half and full cells, matching the candidate's salt and concentration. [0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5::child0]
- Solvent system is EC/PC at 1:1 by volume：Same methods text specifies 'ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume)', identical to the candidate's solvent ratio and basis. [0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5::child0]
- Full cell chemistry is Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 vs hard carbon：The source reports a Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3/HC full cell with this electrolyte and cathode/anode weight ratio 2.5, matching the target system. [0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5]
- Reversible no-plating capacity limit of hard carbon at -20 C：Optical/XRD evidence shows plating begins around 300 mAh/g and a safe capacity within 250 mAh/g is stated for HC at -20 C, giving a no-plating limit in this electrolyte. [0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec7::child0]
- Electrolyte appropriate for stable low-temperature full-cell operation：With this exact electrolyte the full cell shows fast capacity fading at -20 C from increased resistance and continuous Na consumption, and the authors explicitly call for electrolyte optimization to build a stable low-temperature SEI, so it is not shown to be an appropriate low-temperature electrolyte. [0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec6::child19]
- No-plating limit established on the target full cell rather than only the half cell：The 250 mAh/g no-plating result is observed on HC (half cell) via in situ XRD/optical imaging; the source only transfers it to the full cell indirectly through unchanged N/P ratio, without a full-cell plating observation. - c1-1M-NaClO4-EC-PC：The candidate matches the literature electrolyte that establishes the ~250 mAh/g no-plating HC limit at -20 C, so it is a valid starting point, but the same source reports fast full-cell capacity fading at -20 C with this electrolyte and explicitly calls for electrolyte optimization; therefore it is not yet demonstrated as an appropriate low-temperature full-cell electrolyte and no recommendation is made.
- c1-1M-NaClO4-EC-PC：Electrolyte appropriate for stable low-temperature full-cell operation：With this exact electrolyte the full cell shows fast capacity fading at -20 C from increased resistance and continuous Na consumption, and the authors explicitly call for electrolyte optimization to build a stable low-temperature SEI, so it is not shown to be an appropriate low-temperature electrolyte.
- c1-1M-NaClO4-EC-PC：No-plating limit established on the target full cell rather than only the half cell：The 250 mAh/g no-plating result is observed on HC (half cell) via in situ XRD/optical imaging; the source only transfers it to the full cell indirectly through unchanged N/P ratio, without a full-cell plating observation.
- c1-1M-NaClO4-EC-PC：A measured reversible full-cell capacity at -20 C with this electrolyte (only half-cell capacity of ~80% and full-cell fading are reported)
- c2-NPMV-1M-NaClO4-PC-MB-VC：The electrolyte composition, hard-carbon compatibility, and -20 C operation are documented, but the literature only demonstrates this electrolyte with PB (and NFM) cathodes, not with the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode, and no source provides a reversible no-plating capacity limit. The candidate therefore cannot be recommended for the stated target cell on current evidence; a held decision is appropriate pending cathode-specific and plating-limit evidence.
- c2-NPMV-1M-NaClO4-PC-MB-VC：Compatibility with the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode in the full cell：All full-cell data use PB (Prussian blue) or NFM cathodes; no source reports the NPMV electrolyte with a Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode, so this candidate-to-target pairing is untested.
- c2-NPMV-1M-NaClO4-PC-MB-VC：Determination of a reversible no-plating (sodium-dendrite-free) capacity limit：The sources report capacity, retention, rate and thermal data but contain no plating/stripping observation, no anode-potential threshold, and no defined no-plating capacity limit for this electrolyte.
- c2-NPMV-1M-NaClO4-PC-MB-VC：Direct evidence that the NPMV electrolyte supports a Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode in the target full cell
- c2-NPMV-1M-NaClO4-PC-MB-VC：Any no-plating / sodium-deposition-free capacity limit measurement (plating onset, anode potential, or equivalent validation)
- c3-1.0M-NaPF6-DME-G1：The electrolyte candidate itself is well supported for hard-carbon and low-temperature full-cell cycling in G1, but the central deliverable of the original question - a reversible no-plating capacity limit at -20 °C - has no supporting evidence, and the source cathode is only labeled 'NVP/C' without confirming the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 composition; with no recorded tool predictions to bridge this gap, the candidate cannot yet be recommended for the stated workflow goal.
- c3-1.0M-NaPF6-DME-G1：Full cell must pair the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode with hard carbon in this electrolyte.：The full cell is assembled with a cathode only designated 'NVP/C' (NASICON-type, ~3.3 V plateau) and the composition Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 is never stated; the ~3.3 V plateau and the 'NVP' label do not establish that this is the same fluorophosphate composition as the target cell, so the cathode identity match cannot be confirmed.
- c3-1.0M-NaPF6-DME-G1：Evidence on a reversible no-plating capacity limit (absence of sodium plating) for the target full cell at -20 °C.：No source chunk reports plating/stripping, a plating-free capacity ceiling, or any negative-test observation of sodium deposition for this cell; the available data are cycling/rate capacities only, and no recorded tool predictions exist for this candidate.
- c3-1.0M-NaPF6-DME-G1：A reversible no-plating capacity limit for the Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3||hard-carbon full cell at -20 °C: no source reports sodium plating/stripping or a plating-free capacity ceiling, and no computation for this candidate was recorded.
- c3-1.0M-NaPF6-DME-G1：Explicit confirmation that the source's 'NVP/C' cathode is the same Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 composition specified for the target cell.
- c4-1M-NaPF6-diglyme：The candidate electrolyte (1 M NaPF6/diglyme) is the electrolyte used in a related Na-rich NVP/hard-carbon Na-ion full cell with -20 C data, but the sources do not pair it with the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode and provide no quantified reversible no-plating capacity limit; no task computations were recorded, so the no-plating limit and electrolyte suitability for the target cell remain undetermined and a recommendation is held.
- c4-1M-NaPF6-diglyme：Direct evidence for the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 fluorophosphate cathode with this electrolyte：All electrolyte/full-cell results in these sources use Na-rich NVP (Na4VP/Na3V2(PO4)3) cathodes; Na3V2(PO4)2F3 appears only in a literature comparison table with a different anode/context, so the target NVPF chemistry is not paired with NaPF6/diglyme.
- c4-1M-NaPF6-diglyme：A quantified reversible no-plating capacity limit at -20 C：The sources only give qualitative plating statements (anode capacity kept ~5 wt.% above cathode to avoid Na plating; plating accelerates beyond 1 C) and no numerical reversible no-plating limit at -20 C.

- c6-NaPF6-DME-NVPF-fullcell：A reversible no-plating capacity limit (absence of sodium plating) at -20 C for the full cell：The sources report specific capacities and cycling at -20 C but never discuss sodium plating or a no-plating capacity threshold, so the central deliverable is not evidenced.

- c7-1M-NaPF6-PC-EMC-FEC-DTD-PFPN：The candidate's composition matches a literature-reported low-temperature PFPN electrolyte, but that evidence comes from NFM-HC pouch cells at 0 C and no-plating is reported only qualitatively; with the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3 cathode and -20 C unaddressed and no current-task computations recorded, a recommendation is not warranted, so the decision is held pending evidence for the target cathode and -20 C no-plating capacity limit.
- c7-1M-NaPF6-PC-EMC-FEC-DTD-PFPN：Cathode chemistry is Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3：The source's cathode active material is NFM, not the target Na3.5V2(PO4)2F3; the electrolyte evidence therefore belongs to a different cathode chemistry and cannot be transferred to the target cathode without an explicit bridging argument.

source_refs.raw_quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

source_refs.raw_quote: The optical images in Figure S6 clearly indicate the formation of Na metal at the capacity of $350\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ . Sodium dendrite could be recognized at the capacity of $450\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ . The above results suggest that sodium plating start to intervene around $300\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ , and it will be safe to use HC within the capacity of $250\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ at $-20^{\circ}$ C. The performance of the electrode is not only affected by the active materials but also governed by the other components such as electrolyte and binder. It has been demonstrated by Palacín et al. the importance of electrolyte formulation for the stable performance of HC at low temperature. $^{[21]}$ The binder plays a vital role in maintaining the structural integrity, but its effect under low temperature is not clear yet

source_refs.raw_quote: The voltage profiles of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}/\mathrm{HC}$ full cell consists of a plateau at 4.1 V and sloping regime between 3.6-2.5 V, contributing to an accumulative capacity of 306 mAh g $^{-1}$ (based on the mass of anode). The energy density is calculated to be 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ based on the total weight of cathode and anode, along with an average discharge potential of 3.62 V. A stable cyclic performance similar to that in half-cell is achieved at $25^{\circ}$ C, as indicated by full cell F1 in Figure 5b. Ulteriorly, we tested the behavior of full cell under low temperature. Firstly, the performance of $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ half-cell at 0°C and -20°C are measured and given in Figure S7a and S7b. The reversible capacity decreases with lowering the temperature. It maintains 93.2% and 80.4% of the capacity at room temperature for testing at 0°C and -20°C, respectively. Nevertheless, cyclic stability is kept. It is worthwhile to mention that the safe capacity for HC working at -20°C is 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ , which is also around 80% of its capacity at room temperature. Therefore, there is no need to change the mass ratio of the cathode and anode in the full cell for operating at low temperature.

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

source_refs.raw_quote: Glyme-based solvents generally offer a suite of desirable properties, including broad electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity, and compatibility with electrode materials, making them promising candidates for SIB electrolytes [9,10]. Additionally, reducing the coordination strength of the solvent with $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ can accelerate the de-solvation process and enhance compatibility with HC anodes [11]. Modifying the solvent molecule structure appears promising for adjusting the interaction between the solvent and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ [12]. Consequently, we have extended the alkyl chain length of the DME molecule to obtain Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme, as shown in Fig. 1a-d, to investigate the impact of chain length on the electrochemical performance of HC. Electrostatic potential (ESP) diagrams demonstrate a strong interaction between $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and the oxygen atoms of glyme-based solvents, attributed to the localized negative charge on the oxygen atoms (indicated by the blue areas in the calculated ESP diagrams) [13]. For simplicity, the electrolytes (1.0 M) with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ dissolved in DME, Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme are denoted as G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. The freezing points of these solvents, DME at $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Diglyme at $-68^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Triglyme at $-45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Tetraglyme at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , indicate their suitability for low-temperature applications [14,15].

Materials: Commercial NVP (Hubei Ennaiji Energy Technology Co., Ltd. China) cathode and hard carbon (Kuraray Chemical Co., Ltd, Japan) were used as received without further treatment.

The negative electrode was prepared by mixing hard carbon, conductive agent (single-walled carbon nanotube), and binder (carboxymethyl cellulose) at a weight ratio of 0.90:0.04:0.06 dissolved in deionized water. source_refs.raw_quote: As presented in Figure 2c, NaPF $_{6}$ exhibits a relatively low HOMO energy level, indicating its strong stability. The LUMO value of the DME solvent is 1.17 eV, which is higher than those of the ester solvents EC (–0.40 eV), EMC (–0.07 eV), and DMC (–0.14 eV). This suggests that the ether solvent possesses superior reduction stability and is more conducive to the formation of a dense and uniform SEI layer dominated by inorganic species. Figure 2d and Figure S12 illustrate the electrostatic potentials and weak interaction distributions of molecules in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME and $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC electrolyte systems. Regions in red represent relatively positive electrostatic potentials, while blue indicates relatively negative (electron-rich) regions, reflecting localized charge accumulation. In the $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC system, the electrostatic potential range of EMC ranges from -1.59 eV (blue, negative charge) to 1.09 eV (red, positive charge). The non-uniform distribution of polar groups leads to charge inhomogeneity, which can alter the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ and affect the ion migration energy barrier. In contrast, the electrostatic potential range of DME in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME system ranges from -1.48 eV (blue, negative charge) to 0.81 eV (red, positive charge). Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution.

Preliminary electrochemical evaluation (Figure S44) revealed that NVPF exhibits excellent rate capability and stable cycling performance. Figure 8b presents the GCD profiles of the half-cells ( $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//Na and NVPF//Na) and the full cell ( $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//NVPF) at 25°C. The $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//NVPF full cell demonstrates outstanding rate performance at 25°C, delivering reversible specific capacities of 213 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 53 mAh g $^{-1}$ at current densities of 0.5 C and 15 C, respectively (Figure 8c).

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, we developed a synthetic strategy combining a molten-salt method with a vacuum infiltration process to successfully construct a $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC composite with an $Nb-N_{4}$ coordination structure, which was employed as an anode for SIBs. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that $NaPF_{6}$ in an ether-based electrolyte (DME) more effectively promotes the electrochemical performance of electrode materials compared to ester-based electrolytes. The $Nb-N_{4}$ configuration regulates the microstructure and charge distribution of NC, significantly enhancing the pseudocapacitive behavior of $Na^{+}$ storage and enabling fast reaction kinetics. Further investigations and DFT calculations reveal the storage mechanism: the $Nb-N_{4}$ structure promotes the formation of a stable, uniform SEI layer rich in inorganic NaF by lowering the dissociation energy of P—F and C—O bonds in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME electrolyte, thereby improving specific capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability at both room and low temperatures. The optimized $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC exhibits remarkable cycling stability of 238 mAh g $^{-1}$ surpassing 3000 cycles at 10 C (25°C) and exceptional low-temperature capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ (0°C) and 130 mAh g $^{-1}$ (-20°C) at 2 C. 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Low-temperature cyclability is one of the key advantages of sodium-ion batteries. However, reduced kinetics at low temperatures hinder the efficient intercalation of sodium ions into hard carbon, leading to metallic sodium deposition on electrode surfaces, which results in capacity degradation and safety concerns. To address this issue, we investigated the effects of the PFPN additive on low-temperature performance using a 0.4 Ah-level NFM-HC pouch cell. The cells underwent a formation process at a 0.1 C rate, as shown in the formation curves in Figure S1. The charge and discharge curves of both cells were nearly identical. Subsequent EIS analysis after formation revealed that cells with the electrolyte containing 10 wt % PFPN exhibited lower resistance (Figure 1a), indicating that the PFPN additive effectively reduces interfacial resistance in the cells.

The low-temperature cyclability of cells with the baseline electrolyte and 10 wt % PFPN additive was evaluated at 0 °C and 0.2 C rate (Figure 1b–d). Notably, the cell with 10 wt % PFPN additive demonstrated approximately 4% higher capacity retention compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%) after 450 cycles (Figure 1b). During cycling, the average Coulombic efficiency of the baseline electrolyte was 99.939%, whereas the electrolyte containing 10 wt % PFPN achieved 99.951%. Although the charge–discharge curves (Figure 1c) did not immediately reveal significant differences between the electrolytes, the differential voltage curves (Figure S2) highlighted distinct behaviors. The baseline electrolyte exhibited a larger capacity loss in the adsorption–desorption region of the hard carbon anode after cycling (shown in the red area), indicating a reduction in effective adsorption sites on the electrode surface. $^{31}$ Interestingly, we discovered that the PFPN additive effectively suppressed these polarization deteriorations throughout the cycling process. Furthermore, the changes in mid-discharge voltage effectively reflected the polarization variations during cycling (Figure 1d). Generally, the mid-discharge voltage of the cathode gradually decreases during cycling. source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

Predominantly, these coordination structures can be segmented into three distinct categories based on the proximity of cations to an anion: solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIP) with no cations in the immediate solvation shell, contact ion pairs (CIP) involving a single cation, and aggregates (AGG) where the anion associates with multiple cations [6].

source_refs.raw_quote: Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution. This likely results in a looser solvation structure, thereby reducing the desolvation energy barrier for $Na^{+}$ and facilitating faster interfacial ion transport [28]. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to calculate the average coordination number of $Na^{+}$ in the ether-based and ester-based electrolytes (Figure 2e–g). According to the radial distribution function (RDF) analysis, in the $NaPF_{6}$ in EC/EMC/DMC system, $Na^{+}$ preferentially coordinates with the oxygen atoms (O) of the solvents (EC/EMC/DMC), forming an inner solvation sheath. The coordination numbers are 2.46 for EC, 1.50 for EMC, and 1.35 for DMC, indicating that ion-solvent interactions dominate. In the DME-based electrolyte, $Na^{+}$ also coordinates with oxygen atoms, but with a higher coordination number of 4.74. The number of $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions around $Na^{+}$ was determined from the RDF between $Na^{+}$ and F (in $PF_{6}^{-}$ ). Within a distance of r = 0.23 nm, there are approximately $0.85\;PF_{6}^{-}$ anions coordinated to $Na^{+}$ in the ester-based electrolyte, compared to 1.25 $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions in the ether-based electrolyte. This indicates stronger Na–F interactions between $PF_{6}^{-}$ and $Na^{+}$ in the latter system.

source_refs.raw_quote:
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

source_refs.raw_quote: Despite significant advancements in the use of phosphorus-containing electrolytes and additives in laboratory research, their specific mechanisms of action in practical batteries remain poorly understood. $^{25,26}$ This knowledge gap highlights the need for further research to elucidate the mechanisms of performance enhancement by phosphorus-containing components, especially in SIBs, which is critical for advancing their commercialization. $^{27}$ Among these components, ethoxy (pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN) has been widely utilized as an additive to enhance battery safety. $^{28,29}$ In this study, PFPN was introduced into practical pouch-cell-type SIBs to evaluate its effects on cycling performance and capacity optimization under various temperature conditions, thereby redefining the application potential of PFPN additives. These results demonstrate that PFPN significantly improves the low-temperature electrochemical performance of SIBs. Specifically, the incorporation of 10 wt % PFPN enables the battery to retain 85% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at a 0.2 C rate at 0 °C. During electrochemical cycling, PFPN facilitates the formation of a unique SEI layer enriched with phosphorus and nitrogen elements, which improves the kinetic performance of the battery.

citations.chunk_id: 0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5::child0
citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

citations.chunk_id: 0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec7::child0
citations.quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

citations.quote: The long-term cycling stability at -20 °C is tested in Figures 5c and S24; the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte exhibits a high capacity of 80.0 mAh g $^{-1}$ and a capacity retention of 78.5% after 50 cycles, in sharp contrast to the 35.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 74.5% in the NPV electrolyte. Meanwhile, as shown in Figure S25, PB||HC full cells with the NPMV electrolyte also demonstrate a higher discharge capacity during the constant-temperature charge-discharge tests at 100 °C and -20 °C. As for the high-temperature application, the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte exhibits higher capacities at 55 °C, ranging from 123.89 to 103.08 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1–1.5 C (Figures 5d and S26). Noticeably, rapid capacity degradation with fluctuating charge-discharge curves is presented in the NPV electrolyte at 1.5 C, which is attributed to the severe side reactions at high temperature. Furthermore, the rate performance is analyzed and summarized in Figure 5e, where the NPMV electrolyte demonstrates higher capacity retention and smaller overpotentials at varying rates. And this phenomenon is well suppressed in the electrolyte with the MB cosolvent. Therefore, stable long-term cycling with a high capacity retention of 82.9% after 200 cycles is observed in the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte at 55 °C, in sharp contrast with 59.7% in the NPV electrolyte (Figure 5f,g).

citations.quote: Glyme-based solvents generally offer a suite of desirable properties, including broad electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity, and compatibility with electrode materials, making them promising candidates for SIB electrolytes [9,10]. Additionally, reducing the coordination strength of the solvent with $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ can accelerate the de-solvation process and enhance compatibility with HC anodes [11]. Modifying the solvent molecule structure appears promising for adjusting the interaction between the solvent and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ [12]. Consequently, we have extended the alkyl chain length of the DME molecule to obtain Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme, as shown in Fig. 1a-d, to investigate the impact of chain length on the electrochemical performance of HC. Electrostatic potential (ESP) diagrams demonstrate a strong interaction between $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and the oxygen atoms of glyme-based solvents, attributed to the localized negative charge on the oxygen atoms (indicated by the blue areas in the calculated ESP diagrams) [13]. For simplicity, the electrolytes (1.0 M) with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ dissolved in DME, Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme are denoted as G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. The freezing points of these solvents, DME at $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Diglyme at $-68^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Triglyme at $-45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Tetraglyme at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , indicate their suitability for low-temperature applications [14,15].

As depicted in Fig. S18a, even at such low temperature, the HC electrode can still deliver a high ICE of 60.7 % and a reversible capacity of 257.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles at 0.1 A g $^{-1}$ , indicating robust low-temperature performance. Compared with the maximum capacity (258.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) obtained during the initial activation, the capacity retention is as high as 99.4 %. This is further corroborated by the discharge/charge profiles (Fig. S18b), where the closely overlapping curves suggest high electrochemical reversibility [50]. The rate capability tests show that a reversible capacity of 161.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at a high current density of 5.0 A g $^{-1}$ could be still achieved at -20°C (Fig. 5g), with the rate profiles in Fig. S19 confirming consistent excellent rate capability. Moreover, the effective coupling between the HC electrode and G1 is also evident from its performance at 1.0 A g $^{-1}$ , achieving a reversible capacity of 216.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 300 cycles (Fig. 5h and Fig. S20). In principle, the MD simulations suggest that the weak interaction between Na $^{+}$ and DME facilitates rapid de-solvation [6]. citations.quote: S6, showing values of -86.24, -117.93, -109.49, and -160.06 kcal mol $^{-1}$ for G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. These values indicate an easier de-solvation process in G1. Moreover, the ionic diffusion coefficients also vary across the four electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2i, the simulated self-diffusion coefficient of Na $^{+}$ in G1 (1.251×10 $^{-5}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ) is higher than those in G2 (4.829×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), G3 (2.210×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), and G4 (1.525×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), which aligns with the conductivity measurements shown in Fig. S7. In summary, glyme-based electrolytes with shorter chain lengths facilitate rapid de-solvation and efficient ionic diffusion (Fig. 2j), thus enhancing interfacial kinetics and promoting the formation of an anion-derived SEI, thereby contributing to improved electrochemical performance of the target electrode [7,25]. The above MD simulations, complemented by characterizations, have shed light on the nuanced interplay between sodium ion and solvents, and this interplay consequently affects the coordination structures in electrolytes. Predominantly, these coordination structures can be segmented into three distinct categories based on the proximity of cations to an anion: solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIP) with no cations in the immediate solvation shell, contact ion pairs (CIP) involving a single cation, and aggregates (AGG) where the anion associates with multiple cations [6].

citations.quote: Fig. 3c-f present high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of HC electrodes after cycling in different electrolyte to observe their SEI layers. It is found that the transparent coating layers can be observed on all the electrode surface, in contrast to the smooth surface of HC shown in Fig. S9, indicates the formation of SEI layers [28]. The SEI layers generated in G1 and G2 are notably more uniform and exhibit closer contact with the HC surface compared to those generated in G3 and G4. This enhanced uniformity and adherence provides effective protection for the electrode and ensure stable electrochemical performance for sodium storage [29,30]. To ascertain the chemical composition of the SEI layers, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses were performed on cycled HC electrodes. Variations in peak intensities and binding energies were analyzed to distinguish the inorganic and organic components of the SEI layers formed in different electrolytes. Fig. 3g displays the C 1 s, O 1 s, and F 1 s spectra of the SEI layer formed in G1. Deconvolution of the C 1 s spectrum reveals four peaks at approximately 289.4 (RCO₃), 286.3 (C=O), 283.8 (C-O), and 283.4 (C-C/C-H) eV, indicative of decomposed products of sodium salts, solvent-induced polymerizations, polyethylene oxide oligomers, and polyolefin, respectively [11,31].

citations.quote: The NVP cathode electrodes were immersed in 0.5 M Na-Bp complex solution (0.5 M biphenyl in DME) for 10, 30, and 60 s. The cathode electrodes were then washed with DME solvent five times to remove the residual salts followed by evaporation of DME solvent in the vacuum chamber of the glove box for at least 2 h. The electrolyte was 1 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in diglyme and 1 M $NaClO_{4}$ in EC/DEC, V/V: 1:1. Before the preparation of the electrolyte, the salts were dried at 120 °C for 24 h in the vacuum chamber of the glove box. The solvents were dried using 4 Å molecular sieves for 48 h in the glove box. Electrochemical Measurements: Half-cell was assembled using a Na metal, a piece of Celgard 2325 separator, a piece of Whatman glass fiber separator (GF/C), 40 $\mu$ l electrolyte, spacer, and gasket in CR2032-type coin-cell. For the cathode, the testing voltage window was 2.7–3.8 or 1–3.8 V versus Na/Na $^{+}$ under different C-rate (1 C = 117 mAh g $^{-1}$ ). citations.quote: The HC//NFPP full cell shows stable cycling performance over 100 cycles with a high average CE (Figure S12, Supporting Information), indicating the high combability of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte in the full cells. An Ah-level HC//NFPP pouch cells were further assembled to test the feasibility of the practical application of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte. The HC//NFPP pouch cell delivers a reversible capacity of 1.029 Ah and ICE of 82.5% (Figure 3a). Meanwhile, the pouch cell exhibits excellent cycling stability with no swelling during the cycling process. Specifically, the pouch cell manifests a high capacity retention of 80% after 500 cycles at a current rate of 1 C, along with a high average CE of 99.9% (Figure 3b). Moreover, the pouch cell shows stable performance at different temperatures. The discharge capacities are 0.985, 0.884, and 1.06 Ah at -20, -40, and 60 °C (0.1 C), corresponding to 95.7%, 85.9%, and 103% of the capacity retention, respectively (Figure 3c). Even at a higher discharge rate of 0.5 C at 60 °C, the battery can still maintain 103% of its capacity at 25 °C (Figure S13, Supporting Information). The HC//NFPP pouch cell shows outstanding cycling stability at -20 and 60 °C with high capacity retention over hundreds of cycles (Figure 3d,e; Figure S14, Supporting Information). These results indicated the high combability of NaDFOB-G2 electrolytes for practical pouch cells.

citations.quote:
To show the potential for low-temperature application, the NFPP electrodes with different electrolytes were tested at low temperatures. Notably, the NFPP electrode with NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte exhibits a capacity retention of 92.7% at -20 °C compared to that at 25 °C. Even at -40 °C, a high capacity retention of 84.8% is achieved (Figure 2g,h). Impressively, the NFPP electrode with the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte retains higher capacity retention than that with $NaPF_{6}-G2$ electrolyte at both -20 and -40 °C (Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Moreover, the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte works well with other cathode materials. Both the $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}}$ electrodes show high cycling stability over 200 cycles (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Information). Additionally, the compatibility of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte with the hard carbon (HC) anode is also evaluated. The HC electrode has a large overpotential at room temperature and shows a small capacity (Figure S10, Supporting Information), which may be result of the thick SEI film on the Na metal surface slowing down the speed of sodium-ions passing through the SEI film and increase the polarization of the cell (Figure S11, Supporting Information). $^{[8]}$

To avoid the influence of the high polarization from Na metal, HC//NFPP full coin-cells were assembled.

citations.quote: In summary, we developed a synthetic strategy combining a molten-salt method with a vacuum infiltration process to successfully construct a $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC composite with an $Nb-N_{4}$ coordination structure, which was employed as an anode for SIBs. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that $NaPF_{6}$ in an ether-based electrolyte (DME) more effectively promotes the electrochemical performance of electrode materials compared to ester-based electrolytes. The $Nb-N_{4}$ configuration regulates the microstructure and charge distribution of NC, significantly enhancing the pseudocapacitive behavior of $Na^{+}$ storage and enabling fast reaction kinetics. Further investigations and DFT calculations reveal the storage mechanism: the $Nb-N_{4}$ structure promotes the formation of a stable, uniform SEI layer rich in inorganic NaF by lowering the dissociation energy of P—F and C—O bonds in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME electrolyte, thereby improving specific capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability at both room and low temperatures. The optimized $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC exhibits remarkable cycling stability of 238 mAh g $^{-1}$ surpassing 3000 cycles at 10 C (25°C) and exceptional low-temperature capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ (0°C) and 130 mAh g $^{-1}$ (-20°C) at 2 C. In practical applications, a full cell assembled with NVPF cathode and $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC anode achieves an energy density of 230 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and a power density of 6.69 kW kg $^{-1}$ .

citations.quote: As presented in Figure 2c, NaPF $_{6}$ exhibits a relatively low HOMO energy level, indicating its strong stability. The LUMO value of the DME solvent is 1.17 eV, which is higher than those of the ester solvents EC (–0.40 eV), EMC (–0.07 eV), and DMC (–0.14 eV). This suggests that the ether solvent possesses superior reduction stability and is more conducive to the formation of a dense and uniform SEI layer dominated by inorganic species. Figure 2d and Figure S12 illustrate the electrostatic potentials and weak interaction distributions of molecules in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME and $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC electrolyte systems. Regions in red represent relatively positive electrostatic potentials, while blue indicates relatively negative (electron-rich) regions, reflecting localized charge accumulation. In the $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC system, the electrostatic potential range of EMC ranges from -1.59 eV (blue, negative charge) to 1.09 eV (red, positive charge). The non-uniform distribution of polar groups leads to charge inhomogeneity, which can alter the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ and affect the ion migration energy barrier. In contrast, the electrostatic potential range of DME in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME system ranges from -1.48 eV (blue, negative charge) to 0.81 eV (red, positive charge). Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution.

citations.quote: Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution. This likely results in a looser solvation structure, thereby reducing the desolvation energy barrier for $Na^{+}$ and facilitating faster interfacial ion transport [28]. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to calculate the average coordination number of $Na^{+}$ in the ether-based and ester-based electrolytes (Figure 2e–g). According to the radial distribution function (RDF) analysis, in the $NaPF_{6}$ in EC/EMC/DMC system, $Na^{+}$ preferentially coordinates with the oxygen atoms (O) of the solvents (EC/EMC/DMC), forming an inner solvation sheath. The coordination numbers are 2.46 for EC, 1.50 for EMC, and 1.35 for DMC, indicating that ion-solvent interactions dominate. In the DME-based electrolyte, $Na^{+}$ also coordinates with oxygen atoms, but with a higher coordination number of 4.74. The number of $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions around $Na^{+}$ was determined from the RDF between $Na^{+}$ and F (in $PF_{6}^{-}$ ). Within a distance of r = 0.23 nm, there are approximately $0.85\;PF_{6}^{-}$ anions coordinated to $Na^{+}$ in the ester-based electrolyte, compared to 1.25 $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions in the ether-based electrolyte. This indicates stronger Na–F interactions between $PF_{6}^{-}$ and $Na^{+}$ in the latter system.

citations.quote:
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

citations.quote: Despite significant advancements in the use of phosphorus-containing electrolytes and additives in laboratory research, their specific mechanisms of action in practical batteries remain poorly understood. $^{25,26}$ This knowledge gap highlights the need for further research to elucidate the mechanisms of performance enhancement by phosphorus-containing components, especially in SIBs, which is critical for advancing their commercialization. $^{27}$ Among these components, ethoxy (pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN) has been widely utilized as an additive to enhance battery safety. $^{28,29}$ In this study, PFPN was introduced into practical pouch-cell-type SIBs to evaluate its effects on cycling performance and capacity optimization under various temperature conditions, thereby redefining the application potential of PFPN additives. These results demonstrate that PFPN significantly improves the low-temperature electrochemical performance of SIBs. Specifically, the incorporation of 10 wt % PFPN enables the battery to retain 85% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at a 0.2 C rate at 0 °C. During electrochemical cycling, PFPN facilitates the formation of a unique SEI layer enriched with phosphorus and nitrogen elements, which improves the kinetic performance of the battery.

evidence_ledger.quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

Materials: Commercial NVP (Hubei Ennaiji Energy Technology Co., Ltd. China) cathode and hard carbon (Kuraray Chemical Co., Ltd, Japan) were used as received without further treatment.

The cathode electrode was prepared by mixing active materials (NVP), conductive agent (single-walled carbon nanotube), and binder (carboxymethyl cellulose) at a weight ratio of 0.95:0.02:0.03 dissolved in deionized water. The negative electrode was prepared by mixing hard carbon, conductive agent (single-walled carbon nanotube), and binder (carboxymethyl cellulose) at a weight ratio of 0.90:0.04:0.06 dissolved in deionized water. The excess Na compensates for the Na loss and introduces a small amount of Na metal in the carbon host to extend the cell's cycle life. There should be noted that we used $\mathrm{NaPF}_6/$ diglyme electrolytes instead of conventional ester-based electrolytes because the ester-based electrolyte is not ideal for Na metal anode and Na-free Na-metal cells. We tested the CE of Na metal anode and Na-free Na-metal full cell in the ester-based electrolyte (ethylene carbonate/diethyl carbonate, EC/DEC-based electrolyte, Figure S13, Supporting Information). The results indicate the low CE of the Na metal anode and poor cycle life of Na-free Na-metal full cells in the ester-based electrolyte. Therefore, we utilized $\mathrm{NaPF}_6/$ diglyme electrolyte in this work.

evidence_ledger.quote: Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution. This likely results in a looser solvation structure, thereby reducing the desolvation energy barrier for $Na^{+}$ and facilitating faster interfacial ion transport [28]. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to calculate the average coordination number of $Na^{+}$ in the ether-based and ester-based electrolytes (Figure 2e–g). According to the radial distribution function (RDF) analysis, in the $NaPF_{6}$ in EC/EMC/DMC system, $Na^{+}$ preferentially coordinates with the oxygen atoms (O) of the solvents (EC/EMC/DMC), forming an inner solvation sheath. The coordination numbers are 2.46 for EC, 1.50 for EMC, and 1.35 for DMC, indicating that ion-solvent interactions dominate. In the DME-based electrolyte, $Na^{+}$ also coordinates with oxygen atoms, but with a higher coordination number of 4.74. The number of $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions around $Na^{+}$ was determined from the RDF between $Na^{+}$ and F (in $PF_{6}^{-}$ ). Within a distance of r = 0.23 nm, there are approximately $0.85\;PF_{6}^{-}$ anions coordinated to $Na^{+}$ in the ester-based electrolyte, compared to 1.25 $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions in the ether-based electrolyte. This indicates stronger Na–F interactions between $PF_{6}^{-}$ and $Na^{+}$ in the latter system.

evidence_ledger.quote:
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

evidence_ledger.quote: Despite significant advancements in the use of phosphorus-containing electrolytes and additives in laboratory research, their specific mechanisms of action in practical batteries remain poorly understood. $^{25,26}$ This knowledge gap highlights the need for further research to elucidate the mechanisms of performance enhancement by phosphorus-containing components, especially in SIBs, which is critical for advancing their commercialization. $^{27}$ Among these components, ethoxy (pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN) has been widely utilized as an additive to enhance battery safety. $^{28,29}$ In this study, PFPN was introduced into practical pouch-cell-type SIBs to evaluate its effects on cycling performance and capacity optimization under various temperature conditions, thereby redefining the application potential of PFPN additives. These results demonstrate that PFPN significantly improves the low-temperature electrochemical performance of SIBs. Specifically, the incorporation of 10 wt % PFPN enables the battery to retain 85% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at a 0.2 C rate at 0 °C. During electrochemical cycling, PFPN facilitates the formation of a unique SEI layer enriched with phosphorus and nitrogen elements, which improves the kinetic performance of the battery.

citations.chunk_id: 0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec5::child0
citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

citations.chunk_id: 0036_Lin 等 - 2019 - Exploring room- and low-temperature performance of hard carbon material in half and full Na-ion batt::sec7::child0
citations.quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

citations.quote: The long-term cycling stability at -20 °C is tested in Figures 5c and S24; the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte exhibits a high capacity of 80.0 mAh g $^{-1}$ and a capacity retention of 78.5% after 50 cycles, in sharp contrast to the 35.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 74.5% in the NPV electrolyte. Meanwhile, as shown in Figure S25, PB||HC full cells with the NPMV electrolyte also demonstrate a higher discharge capacity during the constant-temperature charge-discharge tests at 100 °C and -20 °C. As for the high-temperature application, the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte exhibits higher capacities at 55 °C, ranging from 123.89 to 103.08 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1–1.5 C (Figures 5d and S26). Noticeably, rapid capacity degradation with fluctuating charge-discharge curves is presented in the NPV electrolyte at 1.5 C, which is attributed to the severe side reactions at high temperature. Furthermore, the rate performance is analyzed and summarized in Figure 5e, where the NPMV electrolyte demonstrates higher capacity retention and smaller overpotentials at varying rates. And this phenomenon is well suppressed in the electrolyte with the MB cosolvent. Therefore, stable long-term cycling with a high capacity retention of 82.9% after 200 cycles is observed in the PB||HC full cell with the NPMV electrolyte at 55 °C, in sharp contrast with 59.7% in the NPV electrolyte (Figure 5f,g).

citations.quote: Glyme-based solvents generally offer a suite of desirable properties, including broad electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity, and compatibility with electrode materials, making them promising candidates for SIB electrolytes [9,10]. Additionally, reducing the coordination strength of the solvent with $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ can accelerate the de-solvation process and enhance compatibility with HC anodes [11]. Modifying the solvent molecule structure appears promising for adjusting the interaction between the solvent and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ [12]. Consequently, we have extended the alkyl chain length of the DME molecule to obtain Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme, as shown in Fig. 1a-d, to investigate the impact of chain length on the electrochemical performance of HC. Electrostatic potential (ESP) diagrams demonstrate a strong interaction between $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and the oxygen atoms of glyme-based solvents, attributed to the localized negative charge on the oxygen atoms (indicated by the blue areas in the calculated ESP diagrams) [13]. For simplicity, the electrolytes (1.0 M) with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ dissolved in DME, Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme are denoted as G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. The freezing points of these solvents, DME at $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Diglyme at $-68^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Triglyme at $-45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Tetraglyme at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , indicate their suitability for low-temperature applications [14,15].

citations.quote: Additionally, the electrochemical sodium storage performance of HC in G1 was further tested at -20°C. As depicted in Fig. S18a, even at such low temperature, the HC electrode can still deliver a high ICE of 60.7 % and a reversible capacity of 257.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles at 0.1 A g $^{-1}$ , indicating robust low-temperature performance. Compared with the maximum capacity (258.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) obtained during the initial activation, the capacity retention is as high as 99.4 %. This is further corroborated by the discharge/charge profiles (Fig. S18b), where the closely overlapping curves suggest high electrochemical reversibility [50]. The rate capability tests show that a reversible capacity of 161.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at a high current density of 5.0 A g $^{-1}$ could be still achieved at -20°C (Fig. 5g), with the rate profiles in Fig. S19 confirming consistent excellent rate capability. Moreover, the effective coupling between the HC electrode and G1 is also evident from its performance at 1.0 A g $^{-1}$ , achieving a reversible capacity of 216.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 300 cycles (Fig. 5h and Fig. S20). In principle, the MD simulations suggest that the weak interaction between Na $^{+}$ and DME facilitates rapid de-solvation [6]. Furthermore, anion solvation promotes the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI, and the accelerated interfacial kinetics contribute to high sodium performance at low temperatures [19].

To achieve a balance between the capacities of cathode and anode, it is crucial to accurately establish the specific capacity of NVP/C. As illustrated in Fig. S23, the cycling performance and charge/discharge curves of NVP/C in half-cells, operating at $0.1\mathrm{A}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ , showcase a high reversible capacity of $101.6\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ after 100 cycles. Furthermore, these charge/discharge curves display a near-perfect overlap, thereby indicating exceptional electrochemical performance. Consequently, taking these specific capacities into account, the mass loadings for HC and NVP/C have been precisely regulated to $0.7\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ and $1.0\mathrm{mgcm}^{-2}$ , respectively. As demonstrated in Fig. S24a, stable cycling at $0.1\mathrm{A}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ further confirms the excellent synergy between HC, NVP/C, and G1, delivering a reversible capacity of $96.9\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ after 100 cycles. The corresponding discharge/charge profiles (Fig. S24b) also show a stable plateau at approximately $3.3\mathrm{V}$ [30]. Regarding rate capability (Fig. S24c), the full cell displays average reversible capacities of 99.7, 90.2, 83.1, 72.5, and $55.6\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ at increasing current densities of 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and $3.0\mathrm{A}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ , respectively.

citations.quote: S6, showing values of -86.24, -117.93, -109.49, and -160.06 kcal mol $^{-1}$ for G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. These values indicate an easier de-solvation process in G1. Moreover, the ionic diffusion coefficients also vary across the four electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2i, the simulated self-diffusion coefficient of Na $^{+}$ in G1 (1.251×10 $^{-5}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ) is higher than those in G2 (4.829×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), G3 (2.210×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), and G4 (1.525×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), which aligns with the conductivity measurements shown in Fig. S7. In summary, glyme-based electrolytes with shorter chain lengths facilitate rapid de-solvation and efficient ionic diffusion (Fig. 2j), thus enhancing interfacial kinetics and promoting the formation of an anion-derived SEI, thereby contributing to improved electrochemical performance of the target electrode [7,25]. The above MD simulations, complemented by characterizations, have shed light on the nuanced interplay between sodium ion and solvents, and this interplay consequently affects the coordination structures in electrolytes. Predominantly, these coordination structures can be segmented into three distinct categories based on the proximity of cations to an anion: solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIP) with no cations in the immediate solvation shell, contact ion pairs (CIP) involving a single cation, and aggregates (AGG) where the anion associates with multiple cations [6].

citations.quote: Fig. 3c-f present high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of HC electrodes after cycling in different electrolyte to observe their SEI layers. It is found that the transparent coating layers can be observed on all the electrode surface, in contrast to the smooth surface of HC shown in Fig. S9, indicates the formation of SEI layers [28]. The SEI layers generated in G1 and G2 are notably more uniform and exhibit closer contact with the HC surface compared to those generated in G3 and G4. This enhanced uniformity and adherence provides effective protection for the electrode and ensure stable electrochemical performance for sodium storage [29,30]. To ascertain the chemical composition of the SEI layers, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses were performed on cycled HC electrodes. Variations in peak intensities and binding energies were analyzed to distinguish the inorganic and organic components of the SEI layers formed in different electrolytes. Fig. 3g displays the C 1 s, O 1 s, and F 1 s spectra of the SEI layer formed in G1. Deconvolution of the C 1 s spectrum reveals four peaks at approximately 289.4 (RCO₃), 286.3 (C=O), 283.8 (C-O), and 283.4 (C-C/C-H) eV, indicative of decomposed products of sodium salts, solvent-induced polymerizations, polyethylene oxide oligomers, and polyolefin, respectively [11,31].

An Ah-level HC//NFPP pouch cells were further assembled to test the feasibility of the practical application of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte. The HC//NFPP pouch cell delivers a reversible capacity of 1.029 Ah and ICE of 82.5% (Figure 3a). Meanwhile, the pouch cell exhibits excellent cycling stability with no swelling during the cycling process. Specifically, the pouch cell manifests a high capacity retention of 80% after 500 cycles at a current rate of 1 C, along with a high average CE of 99.9% (Figure 3b). Moreover, the pouch cell shows stable performance at different temperatures. The discharge capacities are 0.985, 0.884, and 1.06 Ah at -20, -40, and 60 °C (0.1 C), corresponding to 95.7%, 85.9%, and 103% of the capacity retention, respectively (Figure 3c). Even at a higher discharge rate of 0.5 C at 60 °C, the battery can still maintain 103% of its capacity at 25 °C (Figure S13, Supporting Information). The HC//NFPP pouch cell shows outstanding cycling stability at -20 and 60 °C with high capacity retention over hundreds of cycles (Figure 3d,e; Figure S14, Supporting Information). These results indicated the high combability of NaDFOB-G2 electrolytes for practical pouch cells.

citations.quote:
To show the potential for low-temperature application, the NFPP electrodes with different electrolytes were tested at low temperatures. Notably, the NFPP electrode with NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte exhibits a capacity retention of 92.7% at -20 °C compared to that at 25 °C. Even at -40 °C, a high capacity retention of 84.8% is achieved (Figure 2g,h). Impressively, the NFPP electrode with the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte retains higher capacity retention than that with $NaPF_{6}-G2$ electrolyte at both -20 and -40 °C (Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Moreover, the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte works well with other cathode materials. Both the $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}}$ electrodes show high cycling stability over 200 cycles (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Information). Additionally, the compatibility of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte with the hard carbon (HC) anode is also evaluated. The HC electrode has a large overpotential at room temperature and shows a small capacity (Figure S10, Supporting Information), which may be result of the thick SEI film on the Na metal surface slowing down the speed of sodium-ions passing through the SEI film and increase the polarization of the cell (Figure S11, Supporting Information). $^{[8]}$

To avoid the influence of the high polarization from Na metal, HC//NFPP full coin-cells were assembled.

citations.quote: We have thoroughly examined its application as a single salt for the electrolytes of SIBs. The NaDFOB facilitates the formation of a dense and robust cathode-electrolyte interface (CEI) layer on the $\mathrm{Na_{3}Fe_{2}(PO_{4})P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode, significantly enhances its cyclability and Coulombic efficiency (CE). Specifically, the NFPP electrode demonstrates an impressive capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles along with an average CE of 99.96%. Moreover, the hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell with NaDFOB-diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2) electrolyte shows an extended cycling lifespan of 500 cycles and commendable low-temperature performance. Our findings contribute to the exploration of affordable and functional sodium salts, thereby advancing the practical implementation of SIBs in various applications.

citations.quote: This regulation induces the formation of a stable inorganic-rich SEI layer, thereby optimizing the interfacial chemical environment. Third, the precise tuning of the interlayer spacing based on atomic-scale coordination engineering creates an ideal pathway for the reversible insertion/extraction of $Na^{+}$ , which significantly improves ionic transport efficiency. Given the favorable performance of the $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC electrode, a SIB full cell, denoted as $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//NVPF, was assembled to assess its practical applicability at both room temperature and low temperatures. $Na_{3}(VPO_{4})_{2}F_{3}$ (NVPF) was employed as the cathode material, while pre-sodiated $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC served as the anode (Figure 8a). Structural characterization of the synthesized NVPF cathode via SEM and XRD (Figure S42 and S43) confirmed a well-defined cubic crystal structure with uniform particle size and high crystallinity, matching the standard reference pattern (PDF#89-8485) [50]. Preliminary electrochemical evaluation (Figure S44) revealed that NVPF exhibits excellent rate capability and stable cycling performance. Figure 8b presents the GCD profiles of the half-cells ( $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//Na and NVPF//Na) and the full cell ( $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//NVPF) at 25°C. The $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC//NVPF full cell demonstrates outstanding rate performance at 25°C, delivering reversible specific capacities of 213 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 53 mAh g $^{-1}$ at current densities of 0.5 C and 15 C, respectively (Figure 8c).

citations.chunk_id: 0041_Liu 等 - 2025 - Single-Atom Nb-N4 Sites Regulate Hard Carbon Interface for Ultrastable and Low-Temperature Sodium-Io::sec11::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we developed a synthetic strategy combining a molten-salt method with a vacuum infiltration process to successfully construct a $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC composite with an $Nb-N_{4}$ coordination structure, which was employed as an anode for SIBs. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that $NaPF_{6}$ in an ether-based electrolyte (DME) more effectively promotes the electrochemical performance of electrode materials compared to ester-based electrolytes. The $Nb-N_{4}$ configuration regulates the microstructure and charge distribution of NC, significantly enhancing the pseudocapacitive behavior of $Na^{+}$ storage and enabling fast reaction kinetics. Further investigations and DFT calculations reveal the storage mechanism: the $Nb-N_{4}$ structure promotes the formation of a stable, uniform SEI layer rich in inorganic NaF by lowering the dissociation energy of P—F and C—O bonds in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME electrolyte, thereby improving specific capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability at both room and low temperatures. The optimized $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC exhibits remarkable cycling stability of 238 mAh g $^{-1}$ surpassing 3000 cycles at 10 C (25°C) and exceptional low-temperature capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ (0°C) and 130 mAh g $^{-1}$ (-20°C) at 2 C. In practical applications, a full cell assembled with NVPF cathode and $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC anode achieves an energy density of 230 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and a power density of 6.69 kW kg $^{-1}$ .

citations.quote: As presented in Figure 2c, NaPF $_{6}$ exhibits a relatively low HOMO energy level, indicating its strong stability. The LUMO value of the DME solvent is 1.17 eV, which is higher than those of the ester solvents EC (–0.40 eV), EMC (–0.07 eV), and DMC (–0.14 eV). This suggests that the ether solvent possesses superior reduction stability and is more conducive to the formation of a dense and uniform SEI layer dominated by inorganic species. Figure 2d and Figure S12 illustrate the electrostatic potentials and weak interaction distributions of molecules in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME and $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC electrolyte systems. Regions in red represent relatively positive electrostatic potentials, while blue indicates relatively negative (electron-rich) regions, reflecting localized charge accumulation. In the $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/EMC/DMC system, the electrostatic potential range of EMC ranges from -1.59 eV (blue, negative charge) to 1.09 eV (red, positive charge). The non-uniform distribution of polar groups leads to charge inhomogeneity, which can alter the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ and affect the ion migration energy barrier. In contrast, the electrostatic potential range of DME in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME system ranges from -1.48 eV (blue, negative charge) to 0.81 eV (red, positive charge). Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution.

citations.quote: Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution. This likely results in a looser solvation structure, thereby reducing the desolvation energy barrier for $Na^{+}$ and facilitating faster interfacial ion transport [28]. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to calculate the average coordination number of $Na^{+}$ in the ether-based and ester-based electrolytes (Figure 2e–g). According to the radial distribution function (RDF) analysis, in the $NaPF_{6}$ in EC/EMC/DMC system, $Na^{+}$ preferentially coordinates with the oxygen atoms (O) of the solvents (EC/EMC/DMC), forming an inner solvation sheath. The coordination numbers are 2.46 for EC, 1.50 for EMC, and 1.35 for DMC, indicating that ion-solvent interactions dominate. citations.quote:
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

citations.quote: Despite significant advancements in the use of phosphorus-containing electrolytes and additives in laboratory research, their specific mechanisms of action in practical batteries remain poorly understood. $^{25,26}$ This knowledge gap highlights the need for further research to elucidate the mechanisms of performance enhancement by phosphorus-containing components, especially in SIBs, which is critical for advancing their commercialization. $^{27}$ Among these components, ethoxy (pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN) has been widely utilized as an additive to enhance battery safety. $^{28,29}$ In this study, PFPN was introduced into practical pouch-cell-type SIBs to evaluate its effects on cycling performance and capacity optimization under various temperature conditions, thereby redefining the application potential of PFPN additives. These results demonstrate that PFPN significantly improves the low-temperature electrochemical performance of SIBs. Specifically, the incorporation of 10 wt % PFPN enables the battery to retain 85% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at a 0.2 C rate at 0 °C. During electrochemical cycling, PFPN facilitates the formation of a unique SEI layer enriched with phosphorus and nitrogen elements, which improves the kinetic performance of the battery.

Low-temperature cyclability is one of the key advantages of sodium-ion batteries. However, reduced kinetics at low temperatures hinder the efficient intercalation of sodium ions into hard carbon, leading to metallic sodium deposition on electrode surfaces, which results in capacity degradation and safety concerns. citations.quote: In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

citations.quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

citations.quote: Glyme-based solvents generally offer a suite of desirable properties, including broad electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity, and compatibility with electrode materials, making them promising candidates for SIB electrolytes [9,10]. Additionally, reducing the coordination strength of the solvent with $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ can accelerate the de-solvation process and enhance compatibility with HC anodes [11]. Modifying the solvent molecule structure appears promising for adjusting the interaction between the solvent and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ [12]. Consequently, we have extended the alkyl chain length of the DME molecule to obtain Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme, as shown in Fig. 1a-d, to investigate the impact of chain length on the electrochemical performance of HC. Electrostatic potential (ESP) diagrams demonstrate a strong interaction between $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and the oxygen atoms of glyme-based solvents, attributed to the localized negative charge on the oxygen atoms (indicated by the blue areas in the calculated ESP diagrams) [13]. For simplicity, the electrolytes (1.0 M) with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ dissolved in DME, Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme are denoted as G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. The freezing points of these solvents, DME at $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Diglyme at $-68^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Triglyme at $-45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Tetraglyme at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , indicate their suitability for low-temperature applications [14,15].
